Chapter 06

Latency and Congestion

On this page
Units before arithmeticWhere the time goesHow a queue growsCongestion control, flow control, and adaptationChoosing which content to sendAbandoning old content safelyWaiting to enter the transportWaiting for delivery to finishReturning to live playbackSources and further reading

Alice can hear the lecture clearly, but her video is several seconds behind the lecturer. Objects are still arriving, and the connection has not failed. The player is receiving old work more slowly than the publisher creates new work.

To understand how this happens, we need to follow the delay through the system. Some delay is unavoidable: capturing, encoding, and transporting a picture all take time. Other delay comes from waiting in queues. Those queues can continue growing even while every part of the system appears busy.

Units before arithmetic

A bit is a binary digit; a byte contains eight bits. Network rates commonly use bits per second, while file sizes commonly use bytes. Here, the prefixes are decimal: one megabit is one million bits.

Measure Meaning Example
Bitrate, in Mb/s Bits produced or carried each second 4 Mb/s of encoded media
Byte rate, in MB/s Bytes produced or carried each second 4 Mb/s = 0.5 MB/s, before transport overhead
Available capacity The rate a path can currently sustain for this traffic A 2 Mb/s path cannot keep up with a 4 Mb/s source
Throughput The transfer rate actually achieved Measure delivered bytes over a stated interval
RTT, in milliseconds Network round-trip time A 40 ms RTT is not a 40 ms playback delay
Playback latency Delay from capture to presentation Includes processing and buffering as well as transit

A connection can have high capacity and a long delay. “Fast” is ambiguous; use the rate or time that explains the problem. Transport overhead also consumes capacity, so media bitrate and network bitrate are not identical.

Where the time goes

Capture-to-display latency includes capture, encoding, network transit, buffering, decoding, and presentation. A relay or operating system can add another queue along the way. Measuring only the network leaves much of the path unexplained.

Consider this illustrative budget for one frame. The numbers are teaching values, not a MoQ benchmark.

Stage Time
Capture 20 ms
Encode 35 ms
Network 45 ms
Playback buffer 80 ms
Decode and display 20 ms
Total 200 ms

Reducing network time by five milliseconds takes this example from 200 ms to 195 ms. Reducing the playback buffer has more room to help, but that buffer has a purpose: it absorbs variation in arrival time. Removing it may turn uneven network delivery into uneven playback.

The appropriate balance depends on the interaction. Someone listening to a lecture may accept additional buffering to avoid interruptions. Someone speaking with the lecturer needs responses quickly and may prefer occasional missing video to a growing conversational delay.

How a queue grows

Suppose the publisher produces four megabits each second while Alice’s path carries two. Each second adds two megabits to a queue. After five seconds, ten megabits are waiting, ignoring overhead. Even if production stops at that moment, sending that backlog at two megabits per second takes another five seconds.

If production continues at the same rate, waiting longer makes the problem worse. The application must reduce future work, abandon some queued work, or accept increasing delay. This arithmetic applies whether the transport is MoQ, WebRTC, or something else.

Congestion control limits what the transport sends to avoid overwhelming the network. When capacity falls, the transport reduces its sending rate. That protects the path, but it cannot decide whether Alice would prefer a smaller picture or an old high-resolution one. That is the job of media adaptation. See RFC 9002 §7.

The player might request a lower-bitrate rendition, or the publisher might reduce future encoding quality. Reducing future production prevents further growth; it does not automatically remove an existing backlog. To return near the live edge, the system may also need to skip old content.

Congestion control, flow control, and adaptation

Three mechanisms influence how much data is sent. They solve different problems:

Mechanism Question it answers Example
QUIC congestion control How much traffic can this network path carry? Packet loss causes the sender to reduce its sending rate
QUIC flow control How much stream data is the receiver willing to accept? The receiver stops granting more credit while its buffers are full
Media adaptation How much media should the application produce or request? The player switches from a 4 Mb/s rendition to a 1 Mb/s rendition

Flow control protects the receiver with limits on individual streams and the connection as a whole. It does not measure whether a frame is still worth displaying. See RFC 9000 §4. A player can therefore receive data reliably and within its allowed limits while still falling behind the lecture.

Choosing which content to send

Before discarding content, the sender can choose how to divide the available capacity. In our lecture, preserving audio while reducing video may let Alice continue following the explanation. A scheduler—the part of the implementation choosing which pending data to send—needs to know that preference.

MOQT represents these preferences through priorities and group ordering. In draft-21, a lower numeric priority means more urgent work. Subscriber priority is considered before publisher priority; group ordering helps choose among groups when those priorities are equal. The full scheduling rules are in §5.1.

Priority changes which work waits. It does not reserve bandwidth or guarantee arrival by a deadline. If urgent audio consumes the available capacity, less urgent video may remain queued. That is why scheduling preferences need to be paired with limits on how long old work remains useful. Check the conventions of the API you use: moq-lite and MOQT fields are not interchangeable merely because both are called priorities.

Abandoning old content safely

Suppose video group 41 remains incomplete while group 42 provides a fresh decoding starting point. Finishing group 41 would preserve older pictures, but sending group 42 may bring Alice closer to the lecturer. Independent groups make that choice possible without requiring every preceding picture.

The sender still has to respect the stream’s structure. A reliable byte stream cannot deliver later bytes past a missing section. To abandon a subgroup’s remaining stream data, MOQT resets that stream. A receiver must then use the media format’s dependencies to decide where decoding can resume.

Draft-21 defines two optional delivery timeouts. Their different starting points address different places where data can wait. The following examples use a relay’s local clock and a 100 ms timeout. They are separate examples, rather than two required stages for each object. See §5.2.

Waiting to enter the transport

The object delivery timeout measures age from when the last byte of an object’s header arrives from upstream. At the original publisher, it starts when the application supplies that header. Before handing the object to the underlying transport, the implementation checks its age.

Here the object has already spent too long waiting before transmission. For a subgroup, expiry resets the stream rather than removing a few bytes from its middle. For a datagram, the expired message is dropped.

This check is most effective when the application can still control the queue. If it hands large amounts of data to the transport in advance, expired bytes may already be beyond its reach. Draft-21 therefore recommends minimizing transport buffering and checking expiry before retransmission where the transport interface permits it.

Waiting for delivery to finish

The subgroup delivery timeout starts when the endpoint knows all objects in the subgroup have been published. At a relay, receiving the upstream stream’s FIN provides that information. This timer covers remaining delivery work, including recovery after packet loss.

The transport must reach what the specification calls “all data committed” before the timer expires: its completion state for delivering the data, beyond merely accepting bytes into a send buffer. This concerns transport delivery, not whether the player has decoded or displayed the media. Otherwise, the stream is reset. Unlike the object age check, this timer can expire after the sender has handed all the data to the transport.

For datagrams, the subgroup timeout instead uses the same age check as the object timeout; if both are nonzero, the smaller value applies. Zero disables the corresponding timeout. These rules describe a single hop’s delivery decisions. They do not create a capture-to-display deadline across the whole relay network.

Returning to live playback

After the network recovers, Alice may still be watching frames that reached her earlier. A fresh transport queue does not empty the player’s playback queue. The player needs its own policy for skipping stale decoded frames or moving its presentation clock forward, while respecting audio synchronization and decoding dependencies.

This gives us two places to observe recovery: when fresh objects arrive, and when fresh content is actually displayed. Measuring both distinguishes network backlog from playback backlog.

A useful experiment briefly reduces available bandwidth and then restores it. Watch whether playback returns near live, stays behind, or repeatedly changes rendition. Record interruptions as well as average delay. A large keyframe can briefly exceed the path’s capacity even when the average bitrate fits, so the sequence of events matters.

Use a repeatable recorded source for the first experiment. It keeps scene complexity and encoder load stable while you investigate the network response. Once you understand that run, repeat on real devices and networks, where capture, rendering, and additional queues can change the result.
